Improving Patient Safety
 
How improved drug packaging could provide some answers to patient safety issues
 
Packaging
(A) One of the most prominent design issues in pharmacy is that of drug packages and the patient information leaflets (PILs) included in them. Many pharmacists are concerned that current designs are 'accidents waiting to happen'. The UK government shares this concern and, in 2003, the National Patient Safety Agency created a new role, appointing Colum Lowe, who has 14 years' experience as a designer in the private sector, as head of design and human factors.
 
(B) Packaging design in the pharmaceutical industry is handled by either in-house teams or external design agencies. For packaging design of over-the-counter medicines, which do not have to be dispensed by a pharmacist but can be bought directly from a sales assistant, characteristics such as attractiveness and distinguishability are important and so these are usually commissioned from an external design team. The marketing team prepares the initial brief and the designers come up with six or seven designs. Two or three of these are then tested on a consumer group. In contrast, most designs for prescription-only products are created in-house. In some cases, this may simply involve the company's design team applying the house design and then handing it over to design engineers rather than testing the design on a consumer group. Clearly this process cannot adequately address the needs of the wide variety of patients using medication.
 
Design considerations
(C) In her book Information Design for Patient Safety, Thea Swayne highlighted a multitude of design problems. For example, drugs that look or sound alike can lead to confusion; small type sizes and even the glare on silver-foil packaging can lead to names or instructions being misread. One such example is a drug that was accidentally injected into a patient through the spine (intrathecally) rather than through the veins (intravenously). Investigations following this tragedy attributed some blame to the poor choice of typescript used on the drug container. Furthermore, according to Swayne, real situations in which medicines are used include a parent giving a cough medicine to a child in the middle of the night; packaging should be designed for moments such as these rather than for the ideal world of a hospital.
 
Safety and compliance
(D) Child protection is another area that gives designers opportunities to improve safety. According to the Child Accident Prevention Trust, 70% of children admitted to hospital with suspected poisoning have swallowed medicines, and although child-resistant lids have helped, they are not yet fully effective. There is scope for improving what is currently available, according to Richard Mawle, a freelance product designer who feels it is not just children who are blocked by child-proof closures. 'Many child-resistant packs are based on strength but older people may have the same level of strength as a child,' he explained, and suggested that better designs could rely on cognitive skills (e.g. removing the lid using a three-step process). Mawle also worked on a project which involved applying his skills to packaging and PILs. Commenting on the information presented, he said: 'There can be an awful lot of junk at the beginning of PILs. For example, why are company details towards the beginning of a leaflet when what might be more vital for the patient is that the medicine should not be taken with alcohol?'
 
Design principles and guidelines
(E) Most designers work according to basic principles; for example, certain print styles are known to be more difficult to read than others. Look-alike boxes present the potential for errors and an obvious solution would be to use colours to highlight a larger dosage of a drug. However, according to Thea Swayne, designating a colour to a particular dosage is not recommended because this could lead to the user not reading the text on a box. Design features can provide the basis for lengthy debates. One argument is that if all packaging was white with black lettering, people would have no choice but to read every box carefully. The problem is that trials of drug packaging are few – common signage studies concern road-traffic signs and visual-display units. Although some designers take results from such studies into account, proving that a particular feature is beneficial can be difficult. For example, current UK legislation requires packaging to include the name of the medicine in Braille, but, according to Karel van der Waarde, a design consultant to the pharmaceutical industry, 'it is not known how much visually impaired patients will benefit nor how much the reading of visually able patients will be impaired'. Van der Waarde is sceptical about current legislation and says that many regulatory authorities do not have the resources to handle packaging information properly. 'They do not look at the use of packaging in a practical context – they only see one box at a time and not several together as pharmacists would do,' he said.
 
Innovation
(F) On a positive note, a recent innovation exhibition revealed several new designs. 'The popper' aims to help arthritis sufferers remove tablets from blister packs , and 'Pluspoint' is an adrenaline auto-injector (a device that allows diabetics to inject themselves) aimed at overcoming the fact that many patients do not carry their medication due to its prohibitive size. The aim of good design is to try to make things more user-friendly as well as safer. The guidelines in Information Design for Patient Safety are not intended to be legally binding. Rather, the book's purpose is to create a basic design standard and to stimulate innovation. The challenge for the pharmaceutical industry is to adopt such a standard.

Questions 27–32
Look at the following statements (Questions 27–32) and the list of people or groups below.
Match each statement with the correct person or group, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter, A, B, C or D, in boxes 27–32 on your answer sheet.
NB You may use any letter more than once.
1
27 The elderly would benefit from drug containers that do not require force to open them.
28 Adapting packaging for the blind may disadvantage people who can see.
29 Specially designed containers have not been able to eliminate drugs being swallowed accidentally.
30 Designers have to consider how drugs are used in the home.
31 Governing bodies need to compare different drug containers rather than studying individual ones.
32 Information provided with medicine is not listed in the right order.
  • A Thea Swayne
  • B The Child Accident Prevention Trust
  • C Richard Mawle
  • D Karel van der Waarde

Q27 The elderly would benefit from drug containers that do not require force to open them.

Q28 Adapting packaging for the blind may disadvantage people who can see.

Q29 Specially designed containers have not been able to eliminate drugs being swallowed accidentally.

Q30 Designers have to consider how drugs are used in the home.

Q31 Governing bodies need to compare different drug containers rather than studying individual ones.

Q32 Information provided with medicine is not listed in the right order.

Q38 In the accident mentioned in the passage, what was the 'design consideration' that caused a drug to be given incorrectly?

  • A a printing error
  • B the style of print
  • C an incorrect label
  • D the shape of the bottle

Q39 What do some people say about the use of only black and white as a design feature?

  • A Consumers would dislike this option.
  • B Drug containers would all look too similar.
  • C People would pay more attention to label information.
  • D Partially sighted people would find these colours more helpful.

Q40 Why does the writer refer to 'the popper' and 'Plus point'?

  • A to show that progress is being made in pharmaceutical packaging design
  • B to give an example of pharmaceutical design problems that can cause accidents
  • C to prove that a lot of work still needs to be done to improve pharmaceutical packaging design
  • D to point out that patients need to be more informed about pharmaceutical products

reference:
Q27

干扰 “Do not require force” 对应原文的 “based on strength... better designs could rely on cognitive skills”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “Richard Mawle... suggested that better designs could rely on cognitive skills (e.g. removing the lid using a three-step process).”

解析 题目说老年人会受益于不需要用力打开的药品容器。D段 Richard Mawle 提到许多防儿童包装基于力量（strength），但老人力量可能和孩子一样小，建议设计依赖“cognitive skills（认知技能）”，即不用蛮力，选 C。

Q28

解析 题目说为盲人调整包装可能会不利于视力正常的人。E段 Karel van der Waarde 指出目前的盲文立法不仅效果未知，而且不清楚“reading of visually able patients will be impaired（视力正常病人的阅读会受到多大损害）”，选 D。

干扰 “Disadvantage people who can see” 对应原文的 “visually able patients will be impaired”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...according to Karel van der Waarde... nor how much the reading of visually able patients will be impaired.”

Q29

解析 题目说专门设计的容器未能消除药物被误吞的情况。D段 The Child Accident Prevention Trust 指出尽管防儿童盖子有帮助，但“not yet fully effective（尚未完全有效）”，仍有70%儿童误吞，选 B。

干扰 “Not been able to eliminate” 对应原文的 “not yet fully effective” 和 “70%... have swallowed”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “According to the Child Accident Prevention Trust, 70% of children... have swallowed medicines... not yet fully effective.”

Q30

句子 (Paragraph C) “...according to Swayne, real situations... packaging should be designed for moments such as these...”

解析 题目说设计师必须考虑药物在家庭中的使用场景。C段 Thea Swayne 提出药物使用的“real situations（真实情境）”包括半夜父母给孩子喂药，包装设计应针对这些时刻而非医院的理想环境，选 A。

干扰 “How drugs are used in the home” 对应原文的 “real situations... parent giving... to a child in the middle of the night”。

Q31

解析 题目说管理机构需要比较不同的药品容器，而不是研究单个容器。E段 Karel van der Waarde 批评监管机构“only see one box at a time and not several together（一次只看一个盒子，而不是像药剂师那样几个放在一起看）”，暗示应当对比查看，选 D。

干扰 题目是反向表达，原文是批评现状（只看单个），题目是提出需求（需要比较不同的）。

句子 (Paragraph E) “Van der Waarde... says that many regulatory authorities... only see one box at a time and not several together...”

Q32

解析 题目说随药提供的信息没有按正确的顺序列出。D段末尾 Richard Mawle 质疑为什么公司详情在说明书开头，而更重要的禁忌（如不能饮酒）却不在显眼位置，即顺序不对，选 C。

干扰 “Not listed in the right order” 对应原文对 “company details towards the beginning” 的批评。

句子 (Paragraph D) “Mawle... said: '...why are company details towards the beginning of a leaflet when what might be more vital...'”

Q33

解析 题目说非处方药（Over-the-counter）的初步提案由____撰写。B段提到“The marketing team prepares the initial brief（营销团队准备初始简报）”，proposal对应brief，选 E。

干扰 “Proposal” 对应 “initial brief”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “The marketing team prepares the initial brief...”

Q34

干扰 “Produced by” 对应 “commissioned from... designers come up with”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...these are usually commissioned from an external design team.”

解析 题目说接着几个设计由____制作。B段提到这类药通常委托给“external design team（外部设计团队）”，选 C。

Q35

解析 题目说最后选定的设计展示给____。B段提到其中两三个设计会在“consumer group（消费者群体）”上进行测试，选 A。

干扰 “Shown to” 对应 “tested on”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “Two or three of these are then tested on a consumer group.”

Q36

解析 题目说对于处方药（Prescription-only），____创作设计。B段提到大多数处方药设计是“created in-house（内部创作）”，涉及公司的设计团队，选 D。

干扰 “Created in-house” 指向 “in-house design team”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “In contrast, most designs for prescription-only products are created in-house.”

Q37

句子 (Paragraph B) “...handing it over to design engineers rather than testing...”

解析 题目说设计随后被传递给____。B段提到设计团队应用内部设计后，将其“handing it over to design engineers（移交给设计工程师）”，选 B。

干扰 “Passed to” 对应 “handing it over to”。

Q38

解析 题目问导致给药错误的“设计考量”是什么。C段提到调查将部分责任归咎于药物容器上使用的“poor choice of typescript（糟糕的字体选择）”，typescript即字体样式，对应选项 B (the style of print)。

干扰 “Typescript” = “Style of print”。不是打印错误（A）或标签错误（C），而是字体本身选得不好。

句子 (Paragraph C) “...attributed some blame to the poor choice of typescript used on the drug container.”

Q39

解析 题目问关于只使用黑白作为设计特征，有人怎么说。E段提到一个论点是：如果所有包装都是白底黑字，人们就别无选择，只能“read every box carefully（仔细阅读每个盒子）”，对应选项 C（人们会更注意标签信息）。

干扰 “Pay more attention” 对应 “read every box carefully”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...people would have no choice but to read every box carefully.”

Q40

解析 题目问作者为什么提到“the popper”和“Plus point”。F段开头说“On a positive note（在积极的一面上）”，最近的创新展览展示了几个“new designs（新设计）”，这表明行业在进步，对应选项 A（展示药品包装设计正在取得进展）。

干扰 “Positive note” 和 “innovation” 都是“progress（进步）”的信号。

句子 (Paragraph F) “On a positive note, a recent innovation exhibition revealed several new designs.”
